Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charges, from the ruler to the slave, and the caliphate will stay with Quraish while they uphold the religion, even if two remain.
One may wish to be like only two people: one given wealth who spends it rightly, and one given wisdom who acts on it and teaches it.
Obey rulers, even an Ethiopian slave, and bear what you dislike, but obedience is only in good, as shown when a commander ordered his men into a fire.
Do not seek authority, which brings regret on Resurrection Day and is not given to those who ask; a ruler who deceives or neglects his subjects is denied Paradise.
Allah will expose on Resurrection Day whoever does good to show off and trouble whoever troubles people; Jundab advised eating only lawful food and shedding no blood.
A man asking about the Hour, who had prepared little but loved Allah and His Apostle, was told he will be with those he loves.
A woman weeping at a grave rebuffed the Prophet, not recognising him, and when she came to apologise he said patience is at the first stroke of a calamity.
Qais bin Sa'd served the Prophet like a chief police officer serves a ruler, and the Prophet sent Abu Musa and then Mu'adh to Yemen as governors.
Seeing a man who had become Muslim then reverted to Judaism, Mu'adh refused to sit unless he were killed, calling it the verdict of Allah and His Apostle.
Abu Bakra wrote to his son not to judge between two people while angry, for the Prophet said a judge should not judge in anger.
Angered that an imam's lengthy prayer kept a man from the morning congregation, the Prophet told imams to shorten it, for among the people are the old, weak and busy.
Angry that Ibn Umar divorced his wife in her menses, the Prophet ordered him to take her back and keep her through another period before divorcing, if he wished.
Hind, once wishing the Prophet's family degraded and now honoured, asked if she may feed her children from miserly Abu Sufyan's property, and was told she may, reasonably.
To write to the Byzantines, who read only sealed letters, the Prophet took a silver ring engraved 'Muhammad, Apostle of Allah'.
Umar urged a man refusing pay for public work to take it, as the Prophet bade Umar take unsought money, keep it, then give it in charity, never seeking it.
A husband and wife carried out li'an in the mosque after he asked whether a man finding another with his wife should kill him, and divorce was decreed.
A man confessed illegal sexual intercourse in the mosque; the Prophet turned away until he testified four times, asked if he was mad, then ordered him stoned at the Musalla.
A right awarded in error by the Prophet, who judged by what he heard, is a piece of Fire; he awarded Abu Qatada his slain foe's spoils at Hunain.
Walking Safiya home, the Prophet told two passing Ansar men 'She is Safiya', explaining that Satan circulates in the human body like blood.
Sending Abu Musa and Mu'adh to Yemen, the Prophet told them to make things easy, give glad tidings and cooperate, and said every intoxicant is prohibited.
The Prophet ordered that captives be set free and invitations be accepted.
Rebuking a zakat collector who claimed gifts, the Prophet asked whether he would get them sitting at home, warning that whatever is taken unlawfully is carried on Resurrection Day.
Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhaifa, led the early emigrants and companions, among them Abu Bakr and Umar, in prayer at the Quba mosque.
Over freeing the Hawazin captives, the Prophet said he could not tell who consented, so the people's representatives (urafa) consulted them and reported that all agreed gladly.
Ibn Umar counted praising rulers to their faces and speaking otherwise behind them as hypocrisy, and the Prophet called the double-faced person the worst of mankind.
Hind said Abu Sufyan was miserly, and the Prophet told her to take reasonably from his wealth what suffices her and her children.
A right wrongly won through eloquence is a piece of Fire; the child belongs to the owner of the bed, and a false oath to seize property meets Allah's anger.
A companion promised freedom after his death to his only property, a slave, so the Prophet sold the slave for 800 dirhams and sent him the price.
Answering criticism of Usama bin Zaid's command, the Prophet said his father had also been criticised yet deserved leadership, and both were among those most beloved to him.
The most hated person in Allah's sight is the most quarrelsome one.
Khalid killed and captured men of Bani Jadhima who could not say 'Aslamna', ordered captives killed, Ibn Umar refused, and the Prophet twice declared himself free of Khalid's deed.
While the Prophet made peace among Bani Amr, Abu Bakr led the prayer and stepped back on his arrival; in prayer, men say Subhan Allah to alert and women clap.
After many Quran reciters fell at Al-Yamama, Abu Bakr, urged by Umar, had Zaid bin Thabit collect the Quran from scattered writings and men's memories.
When Abdullah bin Sahl was found killed at Khaibar and the Jews denied it, his kin declined to swear, so the Prophet paid a hundred she-camels as blood money himself.
For a labourer's illegal intercourse with his employer's wife, the Prophet judged by Allah's Book: ransom returned, a hundred lashes and a year's exile for him, stoning for her.
Zaid learned the Jews' writing for the Prophet's letters, Umar and Ibn Abbas used interpreters, some held a ruler needs two, and Heraclius questioned Abu Sufyan through an interpreter.
The Prophet questioned a zakat collector who claimed gifts, asking whether he would get them at home, and warned that whatever is taken unlawfully is carried on Resurrection Day.
Every prophet and caliph has two groups of advisers, one urging good and one urging evil, and only the one Allah protects is safe.
Companions pledged to listen and obey, when active or tired, as far as they could, to observe jihad while alive, and to die; Ibn Umar so pledged to Abdul Malik.

Umar's chosen candidates left the choice to Abdur-Rahman, who consulted for three nights, chose Uthman on condition of following Allah's Laws and the Prophet's traditions, and everyone gave him allegiance.
